title: Level identity is syntactic, not runtime: a wrapper called more than once yields distinct Route objects that the extractor merges into one kept level
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/routes.ts:722-723 (wrapperLevels), routes.ts:686 (callMount returns the literal inside the wrapper body), routes.ts:784/819/956 (wrapped levels), extract.ts:205 (t[k].obj === s[k].obj)
evidence: wrapperLevels returns levelOf(mount.route), where mount.route is the single ObjectLiteralExpression inside the wrapper body (e.g. mifos src/app/core/route/route.service.ts:27-34, `static withShell(routes) { return { path: '', component: ShellComponent, children: routes, canActivate: [AuthenticationGuard] } }`). Every call site shares that ts-morph node, so extract.ts:205 counts it as the same level. At runtime each call returns a new object. Angular's check_guards getRouteGuards reuses a node only when `future.routeConfig === curr.routeConfig`; otherwise it pushes CanActivate for the node and deactivates the old subtree. Fixture run through extractGraph from scratch (ngx-rocket eager layout): shell.ts defines the withShell above with canActivate:[auth]; home.routing.ts has `[Route.withShell([{path:'home', component: Home}])]`; about.routing.ts has `[Route.withShell([{path:'about', component: About}])]`; Home has `<a routerLink="/about">`. Output: `n_home -> n_about must guard=null`. Putting both calls in one table, `[Route.withShell([...home]), Route.withShell([...about])]`, gives the same must. In Angular, /about fails under the first shell object and is matched under the second, so the shell is a different routeConfig, `auth` runs and ShellComponent is recreated. The same applies to an array-returning builder (`section(X)` returning `[{path:'v2', children}]`) called twice under one parent. Corpus impact today is none: in mifos each withShell call sits under a distinct lazy parent (app-routing.module.ts:27,31,59,87,91), so k stops before the shell level, and the 15 mifos must edges are within one call.
consequence: Breaks Claim 3.1 and the ch5-results.tex:1033-1034 statement that a level is kept when source and destination 'pass through the same route object'. The extractor tests node identity, and the router tests object identity. The mechanism was added in a8c7480 for mifos and is wrong for any application that calls a route-building wrapper more than once on the same chain.
fix: Give each callMount call site its own level identity, e.g. key the level on (wrapper literal, call expression), so two calls never compare equal. Only a const route object referenced by name may share identity across chains.

verdict.reasoning:
The mechanism is as the finding describes. callMount (packages/adapter-angular/src/routes.ts:656-685) returns `route: obj`, the single ObjectLiteralExpression inside the wrapper body. wrapperLevels (routes.ts:722-723) turns it into `levelOf(mount.route...)`, and levelOf (routes.ts:112-125) stores `obj` as that syntax node. All three wrapped-level sites (the element branch near 784, the spread branch near 819, and childLevels near 956) attach that same node for every call site. extract.ts:205 then keeps a level when `t[k]!.obj === s[k]!.obj && !params && !always`. Two calls of one wrapper on the same parent chain therefore compare equal.

Angular checks the runtime object instead. In @angular/router 18.2.14, router.mjs:3234 reuses a node only when `future.routeConfig === curr.routeConfig`. Otherwise the else-branch at 3256-3260 deactivates the current subtree and pushes CanActivate for the future path. Each wrapper call returns a fresh object, so the shell's canActivate runs again and its component is recreated.

I reproduced the counterexample by running a scratch fixture through the real extractGraph (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kanetran29-personal-uigraph/d25f151e-9d40-4c0d-b297-fe3be149d56e/scratchpad/shell2.ts):
- With `Route.withShell` returning `{ path:'', component: ShellComponent, children: routes, canActivate:[auth] }` and called once per file (home and about), the extractor emits n_home -> n_about must with guard=null.
- With both calls in one table, it gives the same must.
- Control: two identical hand-written shell literals give may with guard "auth". So by the extractor's own guard model the wrapper case should be may, and the must edge comes only from treating one syntax node as one runtime object.

This breaks Claim 3.1. A guard runs that can refuse, for example because the session expired since the source was entered, so the navigation does not happen on every input. It also falsifies the sentence at ch5-results.tex:1033-1034 that a level is kept when source and destination "pass through the same route object". I found no caveat about wrapper-call identity anywhere in the thesis .tex files.

The corpus measurements are not affected, which I confirmed:
- Running collectRoutes on all six apps, only mifos has a wrapper level: route.service.ts:28, 606 routes, 20 call sites at one per file.
- Only HomeModule is eager (app.module.ts:66). Every other withShell call sits under a distinct lazy parent in app-routing.module.ts, so the level comparison stops before the shell level.
- All 15 mifos must edges stay inside one module's single withShell call: accounting, centers, groups, organization, system and checker-inbox-and-tasks.

Severity is major rather than critical because it is a real soundness hole in the central property, with a realistic trigger (the ngx-rocket-style Shell.childRoutes pattern that mifos derives from), but no measured number changes and the fix is local. Keying the level on the call expression as well as the wrapper literal would close it. A stored const route object would still correctly share identity.

ASSUMPTION: the stock ngx-rocket template has two root-level Shell.childRoutes calls (home, and about wrapping a loadChildren). That is from memory and was not checked against its source.

- Read extract.ts:191-212 (runningGuards; the comparison `t[k]!.obj === s[k]!.obj`).
- Read @angular/router 18.2.14 router.mjs:3226-3270 (getRouteGuards: reuse only on `future.routeConfig === curr.routeConfig`, else deactivate and push CanActivate) and :4959 (default shouldReuseRoute uses the same identity).

- Thesis: ch5-results.tex:1033-1034 states the "same route object" rule; grep for withShell/wrapper/builder across the .tex files finds no caveat on call-site identity.

title: Default runGuardsAndResolvers ('paramsChange') also reruns on matrix-parameter changes; 'no path parameter' does not mean 'cannot change'
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/routes.ts:117-118 (params from the path string only; 'paramsChange' treated like 'pathParamsChange'), extract.ts:205; asserted by guards-run.test.ts:27,38,46
evidence: Angular's shouldRunGuardsAndResolvers handles 'paramsChange' (the default) with `!equalParamsAndUrlSegments(curr, future)`. That compares `snapshot.params`, which include the matrix parameters of the last consumed segment, and `equalSegments`, which compares each segment's `parameters`, and it recurses into parents. Only 'pathParamsChange' uses `equalPath`, which ignores matrix parameters. The repository's own test asserts the unsound case: guards-run.test.ts:27 declares `{ path: 'app', component: P, canActivate: [auth], children: [{ path: 'one', component: L }, ...] }`, L (line 38) has the absolute link `<a routerLink="/app/two">`, and line 46 expects `/app/one -> /app/two` to be 'must'. With the source displayed at `/app;x=1/one`, a declared route since the default matcher ignores matrix parameters, the absolute link builds `/app/two`. The 'app' snapshot's params go from {x:'1'} to {}, so CanActivate(app) is pushed and `auth` runs. A scratch fixture with `settings` (canActivate:[auth]) and children a and b gives `n_settings_a -> n_settings_b must`. Relative links preserve the matrix parameters of ancestor segments, because createSegmentGroupFromRoute rebuilds from the snapshot's UrlSegments. So the counterexample needs an absolute link, navigateByUrl, or a relative link that climbs above the kept level and comes back down. That is why none of the 150 corpus must edges is affected: the kept levels in k8sdash and bitwarden are empty-path (oss-routing.module.ts:681, chrome routing ''), and all 15 mifos links are relative (`['../']`, `['../../']`, `['./requests']`).
consequence: Contradicts ch6-discussion.tex:607-609, which says the parameter rule errs only on the cautious side ('which a parameter that does not in fact change makes too cautious'), and the ch5-results.tex:1034 wording 'no parameter the navigation could change'. A must edge in the extractor's own test suite is refuted under the default router configuration.
fix: Keep a non-empty-path level under 'paramsChange' only when the target is relative and does not climb above that level. For an absolute or URL target, treat any level that consumes a segment as entered. 'pathParamsChange' can stay as it is.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding. Every step holds against the code and the Angular 18.2.14 router source.

1. **The extractor checks path parameters only.** routes.ts:99 sets `params` from the path string alone, by looking for segments that start with ':'. routes.ts:100 sets `always` to false when `runGuardsAndResolvers` is unset, 'paramsChange' or 'pathParamsChange', so those three modes are handled the same way. The finding cites 117-118, but the code is at 99-100 at HEAD; the substance is the same. extract.ts:205 keeps a shared level whenever `!params && !always`, and the guard list at 207-209 then drops that level's canActivate, canLoad, resolvers and canDeactivate.

2. **Angular's default mode also compares matrix parameters.** In router.mjs, `shouldRunGuardsAndResolvers` (3272-3289) handles 'paramsChange' and the default with `!equalParamsAndUrlSegments` (2537-2543). That function compares `shallowEqual(a.params, b.params)` and `equalSegments` (389-390, which compares each segment's `.parameters`), and it recurses into parent snapshots. A snapshot's params include the matrix parameters of its last consumed segment (3674-3676: `{...posParams, ...consumed[last].parameters}`). Only 'pathParamsChange' uses `equalPath` (392-396), which ignores parameters. When the mode says to rerun, `getRouteGuards` (3234-3237) pushes CanActivate for the reused node, and 3252-3253 pushes CanDeactivate as well.

3. **An absolute link drops the matrix parameter.** For an absolute command, `findStartingPositionForTargetGroup` (1016-1017) starts at the root. `prefixedWith` (1129-1160) calls `compare` (1208-1209), which requires equal parameters, so `app;x=1` does not match the command `app`, and `createNewSegmentGroup` builds `/app/two` with no parameters.
   - With the source displayed at `/app;x=1/one`, the 'app' snapshot's params go from {x:'1'} to {}, so `auth` runs again.
   - The default matcher compares only `segment.path`, so `/app;x=1/one` is an address of the declared route.
   - The thesis's own self-loop rule (ch3:154-158) treats parameter and query values as inputs, and the thesis never mentions matrix parameters (grep for 'matrix' finds nothing in any .tex file).

   So the must edge in the extractor's own test is false under the default configuration: guards-run.test.ts:27 (route), :38 (absolute `routerLink="/app/two"`), :46 (expects /app/one -> /app/two to be must). I ran that test file at HEAD and it passes (8/8), which confirms the extractor outputs must for this edge.

4. **Relative links keep the matrix parameter.** `createSegmentGroupFromRoute` (858-874) rebuilds the tree from the snapshot's `url` segments with their parameters, and `../` only replaces the source's own group. That is why the corpus is not affected.

5. **The thesis prose contradicts the implementation.**
   - ch6-discussion.tex:607-609: the reuse rule ('unless its path has a parameter or runGuardsAndResolvers is set') is said to err only on the cautious side ('which a parameter that does not in fact change makes too cautious'). That is false.
   - ch5-results.tex:1034 ('no parameter the navigation could change') and ch3-analysis.tex:150-151 ('reused unless their parameters can change') describe a rule the implementation does not apply.

**Why major:** Claim 3.1 is the only soundness property the thesis claims. The thesis says this rule can only be too cautious, and a must edge in the extractor's own test suite is wrong under Angular's default router configuration.

**What limits it:** none of the 150 corpus must edges is affected, so no measured figure changes. The flaw is in the universal claim, the prose and the test fixture, not in the results.

title: Redirects are matched only by exact full-path key: pathMatch is never read, and a redirect at a parameterised path is not a rival
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/extract.ts:229-234 (redirects.get(path), rival only on an exact key), routes.ts:900-906 (redirects.set(fullPath, …) with no pathMatch); 'pathMatch' occurs in routes.ts only in the comment at :56
evidence: (1) Prefix: Angular's `match()` lets `{path:'', pathMatch:'prefix'}` match every URL at its level and lets a non-empty prefix redirect consume a leading segment. Fixture `{path:'old', children:[{path:'', redirectTo:'/a', pathMatch:'prefix'}, {path:'x', component: X}]}` with a link to /old/x gives `n_a -> n_old_x must`. Angular hits the empty prefix redirect first and never shows X. Real corpus code with this shape: mifos src/app/loans/loans-routing.module.ts:406-414 and savings-routing.module.ts:219-227 (`{ path: ':loanId/charges', children: [{ path: '', redirectTo: '../charges', pathMatch: 'prefix' }, { path: ':id', … }, { path: ':id/adjustment', … }] }`). The redirect rewrites the segments to ['..','charges',…], processSegment runs with allowRedirects=false, ':id' consumes '..' and leaves leftovers, so the whole branch never matches. The extractor still publishes n_loans_loanId_charges_id and n_…_charges_id_adjustment with edges into them, held at may only because those routes carry resolvers. (2) Parameterised redirect: fixture `[{path:'a',…}, {path:'item/:id', redirectTo:'/items/:id', pathMatch:'full'}, {path:'item/new', component: N}, {path:'items/:id', component: I}]` with a link to /item/new gives `n_a -> n_item_new must`. Angular takes the first matching route, the redirect, and lands on I. matchAll counts only screens, and `rival` (extract.ts:233) checks only an exact-key redirect.
consequence: Breaks the 'screens a redirect answers' and ambiguity demotions behind Claim 3.1. Contradicts ch6-discussion.tex:622-626 ('Wherever two declared routes, or a route and a redirect, can answer an address, the edge is held at may'). The extractor can emit must to a screen the router never displays at that address.
fix: Store redirects with pathMatch and the route pattern. In land(), treat any redirect whose pattern prefix-matches (pathMatch prefix) or pattern-matches (':' segments) the path as a rival, and mark it ambiguous unless declaration order is modelled.

verdict.reasoning:
The defect is real, but nothing the thesis measured changes because of it.

Code: `routes.ts:903-906` stores each redirect only under its exact full path (`redirects.set(fullPath, redirectTarget)`). `pathMatch` never reaches that map. In `routes.ts` it appears only in the doc comment at line 56. `extract.ts:229-234` (`land`) looks up `redirects.get(path)` by exact key and treats a redirect as a rival only on that exact key. `matchAll` (`matcher.ts:70`) counts screens only. So a redirect whose pattern has parameters, or one that matches as a prefix, is never treated as a rival.

Angular's real semantics, checked in the router source (`@angular/router` 21.2.12, `fesm2022/_router-chunk.mjs`):
- `match()` at :2790 matches an empty path with `pathMatch` `prefix` against every remaining segment.
- `processSegment` at :2992 takes the first route in declaration order.
- An absolute redirect throws `AbsoluteRedirect` (:2589-2593), so matching restarts and the leftover segments are dropped.
- After a relative redirect, `processSegment` runs again with `allowRedirects=false` (:3044).
- A relative redirect target such as `'../charges'` is parsed literally into the segments `['..','charges']`. Nothing resolves the `..`, so a child at `:id` consumes `'..'`, the rest are leftovers, and the branch fails to match.

I ran the extractor at HEAD (`extractGraph` on an in-memory project) on these fixtures:
- An empty-path child redirect with `pathMatch: 'prefix'` before `'x'`, linked to `/old/x`, gives `n_a->n_old_x` **must**. Angular lands on `/a`.
- `'item/:id'` redirecting to `/items/:id` (`pathMatch: 'full'`) before `'item/new'`, linked to `/item/new`, gives `n_a->n_item_new` **must**. Angular lands on `I`.
- `'old'` redirecting to `/items` with the default prefix match before `'old/new'` gives `n_a->n_old_new` **must**. Angular never shows `N`.
- Control: a redirect at exactly `/item/new` gives **may**.

The thesis text is contradicted in two places, `ch3-analysis.tex:165-167` and `ch6-discussion.tex:624-626` ("a route and a redirect, can answer an address ... held at may"). Neither chapter mentions `pathMatch` or redirects at parameterised paths. `ch3:194-196` concedes that the demotion half of Claim 3.1 is not independently verified, and this is exactly a hole in that half. The witness check would not catch it, because the destination names agree.

Why minor rather than major:
1. None of the 150 corpus must edges is affected. I tested every must edge's destination against every redirect key the extractor collects, both overlapping patterns and paths under a redirect key. The per-app must counts (9, 0, 0, 125, 1, 15) match `generated-census.tex`.
2. Every counterexample needs a declaration order that already leaves the target screen unreachable at its own address, which is a misconfiguration in the application.
3. The real mifos shape the finding cites exists five times (loans charges, savings charges, groups committee, recurring-deposit transactions, fixed-deposit transactions). All 380 edges into those screens are may. The finding says they are may "only because of resolvers", which is inaccurate: 358 carry `AuthenticationGuard`, and the 22 without a guard are demoted for other reasons.

Side note, outside this finding: the route probe's `frameworkAnswer` (`route-probe/framework-answer.mjs`) ignores declaration order and prefix redirects by design. So the "Not mounted = 0" result for mifos does not rule out these unreachable screens, such as `/groups/:groupId/committee/add-role`.

Summary: a genuine counterexample to Claim 3.1 and to the stated demotion rule. The thesis needs either a code fix or a scoped statement or threat-to-validity line, but no measured figure changes.

title: canMatch runs on routes the router tries and abandons, and on the branch a redirect passes through; runningGuards only reads the final target's chain
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/extract.ts:201-212 (canMatch taken from t only), extract.ts:223-241 (land discards the levels of the pre-redirect branch); thesis ch3-analysis.tex:154-155
evidence: In recognize, matchWithChecks runs `runCanMatchGuards` on every route whose path matches, before descending into its children, and redirectIfUrlTree turns a UrlTree result into a redirect. (a) Fixture `[{ path: '', canMatch: [adminOnly], children: [{ path: 'admin', component: Admin }] }, { path: '', children: [{ path: 'a', component: A }, { path: 'b', component: B }] }]` with A linking to /b gives `n_a -> n_b must guard=null`. Every navigation to /b first runs adminOnly on the first empty-path route, and a UrlTree such as /login redirects it. (b) Fixture `{ path: 'beta', canMatch: [beta], children: [{ path: '', pathMatch: 'full', redirectTo: '/new' }] }, { path: 'new', component: N }` with a link to /beta gives `n_a -> n_new must`. beta() runs before the redirect is applied, and if it returns false the address matches nothing. A canLoad on a lazy route whose module redirects outside itself behaves the same way. No corpus instance found: the only canMatch in the corpus is bitwarden individual-billing-routing.module.ts:35,59, on same-path siblings where the first-declared route carries the guard and so already gates.
consequence: Contradicts ch3-analysis.tex:154-155 ('the canMatch of every route its address is matched through' is narrower than what the router runs) and Claim 3.1: the extractor emits must on navigations that run a guard able to refuse or redirect.
fix: In runningGuards, add the canMatch of every route on an earlier-declared sibling whose path prefix-matches the target address, plus the canMatch and canLoad of the levels land() passed through before each redirect hop. Alternatively demote when any such route exists.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds up in the code and in two fixtures run against HEAD. It has no instance in the corpus, so I rate it minor rather than the reported major.

Code:
- `runningGuards` (packages/adapter-angular/src/extract.ts:201-212) builds its guard list only from `levelsByNodeId.get(to)` and the source's levels. The canMatch it collects is `t.flatMap(l => l.canMatch)`, which covers only the target's own chain of route objects.
- `land()` (extract.ts:223-241) follows redirects and returns only `{target, ambiguous}`. Its callers (extract.ts:341/393, 674/680) then pass the final target's nodeId to `runningGuards`.
- In routes.ts:868, a route's `levels` are its ancestors plus itself. They never include an earlier-declared sibling that was tried and abandoned, and never the branch a redirect passed through.

Router semantics (from my knowledge of the Angular source; I did not open it in this check):
- In the router's recognize step, `matchWithChecks` runs `runCanMatchGuards` on every route whose path matches before it descends into the children. An empty path with the default `pathMatch: 'prefix'` matches every address.
- `redirectIfUrlTree` turns a UrlTree from canMatch into a redirect.
- canLoad runs in `getChildConfig` before the module loads; when it fails, `canLoadFails` cancels the navigation.
- An absolute redirect is applied only after the canMatch of the branch has run.

Both fixtures reproduce, written to the scratchpad and run with tsx against src/extract.ts:
- (a) `[{path:'', canMatch:[adminOnly], children:[{path:'admin'...}]}, {path:'', children:[a, b]}]`, with A linking to /b, gives `n_a -> n_b must guard=null`. Every navigation to /b runs adminOnly, and a UrlTree from it redirects the navigation.

title: A function-valued redirectTo on an empty-path child is read as a plain level, so the screen above counts as displayed at its own address
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/routes.ts:900-925 (stringProp(redirectTo) gives null, so redirectTarget === null and the host branch appends a level instead of setting redirectsTo); extract.ts:246 (hidden)
evidence: Angular 18+ accepts `redirectTo: (route) => string|UrlTree`, and the corpus pins Angular 20.3 (mifos package.json:53) and 21.2 (realworld). Fixture `{ path: 'p', component: P, children: [{ path: '', pathMatch: 'full', redirectTo: () => 'c' }, { path: 'c', component: C }] }` with a link to /p gives `n_a -> n_p must`. The router always rewrites /p to /p/c. With a string redirectTo the same fixture would land on /p/c or be demoted.
consequence: Violates the stated demotion 'screens a redirect answers' (Claim 3.1): the must edge names a destination the router never displays at that address.
fix: If redirectTo is present but not a readable string, set host.redirectsTo to an unknown marker, or put the address in `redirects` with an unknown target, so hidden() and land() demote.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds. I reproduced it, and the cause is a little wider than the finding says. In routes.ts:900, `stringProp(obj, 'redirectTo')` (resolve.ts:199-206) returns null for anything it cannot reduce to a constant string. That covers a function value (`() => 'c'`, which Angular 18+ accepts) and also an identifier that is not a constant (`const TARGET = build()`). Lines 903-906 then register no redirect. In the host branch (routes.ts:921-926), `redirectTarget === null` sends the child down the "plain level" path, so `host.redirectsTo` is never set. As a result `redirectOfNode` (extract.ts:214), `land()` and `hidden()` (extract.ts:246) never see the redirect. Nothing else marks the route as unread: the `unreadable` bookkeeping covers only `path`/`matcher`/outlet/spread/subtree losses, never `redirectTo`. So the extractor emits no soundiness note.

The same root cause also breaks a top-level sibling redirect (`{path:'x', redirectTo: fn, pathMatch:'full'}, {path:'x', component:X}`). With a string target that edge is demoted to may; with a function or non-constant target it comes out must. In Angular the redirect route is matched first, so X is never displayed at /x. That contradicts Claim 3.1's demotion "screens a redirect answers", and it falls inside the declared route set.

Corpus incidence is zero. Every `redirectTo` in the six pinned checkouts is either a string literal or a member of an `Object.freeze` constant table, which the resolver unwraps (resolve.ts:713-714, FREEZE_CALLEE). The only non-literal ones are bitwarden's `AuthRoute.SignUp` and `AuthWebRouteSegment.Account`; `AuthWebRouteSegment` is an `Object.freeze` constant and `AuthRoute` is read through the same freeze unwrapping. So no measured number in the thesis changes. It is a soundness hole you can construct within the stated scope, not one observed in the evaluation. Hence minor.

The suggested fix is right in direction. When `propNamed(obj,'redirectTo')` is present but `stringProp` returns null, the route should be treated as a redirect with an unknown target: set `host.redirectsTo` or a `redirects` entry with an unknown marker so that `hidden()`/`land()` demote, or record it in `unreadable`.

title: A route title resolver is an awaited resolver but is not read
evidence: Angular's resolve_data runResolve adds `config.title` to the resolvers when it is not a static string (`if (config?.title !== undefined && !hasStaticTitle(config)) resolve[RouteTitleKey] = config.title`), and the router awaits it like any resolver. Fixture `{ path: 'b', component: B, title: titleOf }` with `titleOf: ResolveFn<string> = () => fetch(...).then(...)` gives `n_a -> n_b must`. No corpus use: ghostfolio's titles are static strings from a constants map (app.routes.ts:37 etc.).
consequence: Contradicts ch3-analysis.tex:158 ('A resolver is awaited by the router and demotes the edge'): an awaited, rejectable resolver leaves the edge at must.
fix: Set resolve=true when `title` is present and not a string literal or a resolvable string constant.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds up. The extractor never reads a route's `title` property: `levelOf` sets `resolve: propNamed(obj, 'resolve') !== undefined` (packages/adapter-angular/src/routes.ts:124), and nothing anywhere in packages/adapter-angular/src mentions `title`.

The installed Angular router (18.2.14) treats any title that is not static as a resolver. In fesm2022/router.mjs, `runResolve` at lines 4107-4118 does `if (config?.title !== undefined && !hasStaticTitle(config)) resolve[RouteTitleKey] = config.title`, and `hasStaticTitle` (line 2544) is true only for a string or null. `runResolve` then calls `resolveNode`, the same path ordinary resolvers take, and runs only for routes the navigation enters. So a `ResolveFn<string>` or a `Type<Resolve<string>>` title follows exactly the `resolve` semantics the thesis describes. It can cancel the navigation: an empty result goes through `isEmptyError` to EMPTY, a thrown error fails the navigation, and a returned RedirectCommand redirects it (line 4126).

Counterexample: `{ path: 'b', component: B, title: titleFn }` where `titleFn` returns `EMPTY` or rejects. `runningGuards` (extract.ts:201-211) reports `resolves: false` because the level's `resolve` is false, so the may condition at extract.ts:398 and 688 is not triggered. An unconditional link to `/b` therefore stays must, yet on that input the navigation does not happen. That breaks Claim 3.1 and contradicts ch3-analysis.tex:158 ("A resolver is awaited by the router and demotes the edge as an await does").

Severity is minor because no corpus app has a dynamic title in its route configuration. Ghostfolio's route titles are a string literal, a $localize template, or a property chain such as `internalRoutes.api.title` (app.routes.ts:37, home-page.routes.ts:42-43). That chain resolves to `$localize` strings in libs/common/src/lib/routes/routes.ts, which are static at runtime. A grep of the routing files in all six corpora found no ResolveFn<string> or class title resolver, so the measured numbers are unaffected. This is a gap in the soundness argument and the extractor's router model, not a measured error.

The proposed fix needs care. A purely syntactic test ("not a string literal or a resolvable string constant") would wrongly demote ghostfolio's property-chain and $localize titles. The right test is whether the initializer is a function or class, for example through the type checker (string-typed means static).

title: canDeactivate on an open auxiliary route is not modelled, and routerLink="/" and navigateByUrl drop the outlet
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/extract.ts:201-212 (s is the primary chain only), routes.ts aux handling (auxHere: aux routes mint no node and no level)
evidence: Angular's createUrlTree with commands ['/'] reaches updateSegmentGroupChildren(root, 0, []), which returns `new UrlSegmentGroup(segments, {})` and drops every root outlet. navigateByUrl('/x') parses a fresh tree. getChildRouteGuards then calls deactivateRouteAndItsChildren on the aux node and pushes its CanDeactivate. Fixture routes `{path:'', component:H}, {path:'a', component:A}, {path:'compose', component:Pop, outlet:'popup', canDeactivate:[leave]}` with A linking to `/` give `n_a -> n_root must`. Source URL /a(popup:compose) is a declared route, the click runs `leave`, and the guard can refuse. This is the same link shape as realworld footer.component.html:3 (`routerLink="/"`, 8 must edges), but realworld declares no aux routes, so there is no corpus impact today.
consequence: Claim 3.1 quantifies over every input on which the code executes. An input with an auxiliary outlet open runs a guard the extractor never sees.
fix: Demote any edge from a screen whose application declares aux routes with canDeactivate when the target is '/' or a URL, or add a soundiness note that scopes the claim to primary-only URLs.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds. Its one inaccuracy is the code path it cites, and the conclusion does not depend on it.

1. **The extractor never sees aux routes.**
   - routes.ts:893 sets `auxHere` for any route on a non-primary outlet. Lines 908 and 919 then mint no screen and no host level for it, so an aux route's canDeactivate is never stored in any screen's `levels`.
   - extract.ts:201-212 (`runningGuards`) builds canDeactivate only from `s.slice(k)`, the primary chain of the source screen. Guards on an open aux outlet can never be counted.

2. **Angular does run that guard.** Checked against the installed @angular/router 21.2.12 (`_router-chunk.mjs`).
   - A routerLink of `/` gives commands `['/']`. `computeNavigation` and `toRoot()` (lines 665-667, 727) return `new UrlSegmentGroup([], {})`, which drops every root outlet. The finding names `updateSegmentGroupChildren(root, 0, [])` as the path; that is wrong, but the effect is the same.
   - `navigateByUrl('/b')` parses a fresh tree, so the aux outlet is dropped there too.
   - `getChildRouteGuards` (line 2275) calls `deactivateRouteAndItsChildren` on the aux child that no longer appears. That function (line 2341) pushes a CanDeactivate for the aux route, so `leave` runs and can cancel the navigation.
   - A non-root absolute link such as `/b` keeps the other outlets (`updateSegmentGroupChildren`, line 838), so the gap is limited to `/` and URL navigations, as the finding says.

3. **The extractor reproduces the bad edges.** I ran the finding's fixture through `extractGraph`: routes `''`→H, `'a'`→A, `'b'`→H, plus `'compose'` on the popup outlet with `canDeactivate: [leave]`. Component A has `<a routerLink="/">` and calls `navigateByUrl('/b')`. Output: `n_a -> n_root must null` and `n_a -> n_b must null`. On the input `/a(popup:compose)`, A's code runs and `leave` can refuse, so both must edges break Claim 3.1 as written.

4. **The thesis text overclaims.** ch3-analysis.tex:153-157 says the guards a navigation runs are decided "the way the router decides it", including "the canDeactivate of every route it leaves". The thesis treats named outlets only as a gap in what the graph contains (appendix-a.tex:650-671). Its aux-outlet demotion (ch3-analysis.tex:168) covers only a target URL that names an outlet, not a source state with one open.

5. **A stronger variant, beyond the finding.** If `/b` is a componentless route with an empty-path primary child and an empty-path popup child carrying `canActivate: [leave]`, the extractor still emits `n_a -> n_b must`. Angular matches empty-path named-outlet children automatically, which is how bitwarden's environment-selector renders, so that guard runs on a plain primary-to-primary navigation.

6. **No corpus impact, so severity stays minor.**
   - realworld has exactly 8 must edges witnessed at footer.component.html:3, matching the finding, and declares no aux routes.
   - A ts-morph scan found 56 route objects with an `outlet` property across alfresco, k8sdash and bitwarden, in files containing `outlet: '...'`, excluding spec and stories files. None contains canDeactivate, canActivate, canMatch, canLoad, resolve or runGuardsAndResolvers.
   - alfresco's one spread aux route (aca-content.routes.ts:79, `...additionalData`) gets only `data` from its callers (line 244).
   - Its lazy AcaViewerModule routes carry no guards.

The claim as stated fails on a fixture, but no measured figure changes. The fix is a scoping or soundiness sentence, or a demotion rule for applications that declare guarded aux routes.

title: Anchors with a target other than _self never navigate the application, but the extractor ignores target; the thesis disclosure misstates this case
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/nav.ts:151,180-183 (STATIC_LINK_RE / templateTargets read no `target` attribute; nav.ts and controls.ts never mention target or _blank); thesis ch6-discussion.tex:616-621
evidence: Angular's RouterLink.onClick does `if (this.isAnchorElement) { if (button !== 0 || ctrlKey || …) return true; if (typeof this.target === 'string' && this.target != '_self') return true; }` and returns before navigateByUrl. So an `<a routerLink="/x" target="_blank">` navigates the current application on no activation at all. The thesis says 'a must edge from an anchor holds for a plain activation and not for these', which is false for target-bearing anchors because no activation navigates. Corpus instance: bitwarden send-access-explainer.component.html:13 `<a bitLink routerLink="/signup" target="_blank">`. Its edge `o_SendAccessExplainerComponent -> n_signup` is may only because of unauthGuardFn() and the unplaced origin. A guard-free placed copy of that markup would be must. For scale: 72 of the 150 corpus must edges are anchor-hosted (realworld 9, k8sdash chrome template.html:30 x62, mifos checker-inbox `<a mat-tab-link>` x1). For those, the plain-activation qualifier in ch6 is the only thing that saves Claim 3.1, and the claim in ch3-analysis.tex:136-139 is stated without it.
consequence: Edges from target-bearing anchors fail Claim 3.1 even under the thesis's own restriction to plain activation. The claim as stated in Chapter 3 is unqualified while 48% of the must tier depends on that qualifier.
fix: Read the `target` attribute on anchor routerLinks and drop the edge, or demote it to may, when target is not _self. State the plain-primary-activation restriction in the Claim 3.1 text itself.

verdict.reasoning:
Two parts of the finding hold up and two do not.

Holds: the extractor ignores the `target` attribute. In nav.ts:151, STATIC_LINK_RE matches only `routerLink="..."`. templateTargets (nav.ts:171-186) sets every routerLink as 'click:routerLink' and never reads `target`. Angular's RouterLink.onClick does return early for an anchor whose target is a string other than '_self', before navigateByUrl runs. I took that from my knowledge of Angular's router_link.ts, because no copy of @angular/router exists anywhere on this machine to check against.

Does not hold:
(1) The claim that the thesis "misstates this case" is wrong. ch6-discussion.tex:616-621 names this exact case: "...and so does an anchor whose target names another context." It then says "a must edge from an anchor holds for a plain activation and not for these". "These" includes anchors that carry a target, so the thesis already says the must edge fails for them. At most the wording is loose, because "plain activation" could be read as covering a target-bearing anchor. That is a phrasing nit, not a misstatement.
(2) No evidence that it matters for the thesis. None of the 150 corpus must edges is witnessed by an anchor carrying `target` in any form, bound or literal. The only corpus example the finding cites, bitwarden send-access-explainer.component.html:13 to n_signup, is already may in the graph (guard unauthGuardFn()). So every measured must-tier figure stays the same. The failure exists only for a hypothetical guard-free copy, which the thesis already discloses.
(3) The "48% of the must tier depends on that qualifier" point concerns modifier-key or non-primary-button activation, not `target`. That is a different limitation, and the same ch6 bullet discloses it.

Residual true point: Claim 3.1 (ch3-analysis.tex:135-139) is stated without the plain-activation qualifier, and Chapters 3-5 have no pointer to sec:limitations. That is a presentation gap about a limitation the thesis already discloses, not a defect in the extractor or the measurement as this finding frames it.

title: Four mifos system-menu must constructs are nested routerLinks whose own navigation is cancelled on every click
evidence: Each inner `<div class="menu-left-section" [routerLink]=...>` (296, 540, 574, 608) sits inside a `<mat-list-item [routerLink]=...>` with the same target (294, 538, 572, 606). The RouterLink listens only to click, and a click on the div always bubbles to the mat-list-item, so the inner construct's navigation never completes.
consequence: The edges still hold, because 294/538/572/606 are must. But 4 of the 25 constructs counted as earning must (\CensusMustSites=25, \CensusMustSitesMifos=19) reach the destination only through an ancestor's navigation. That contradicts extract.ts:301-304, 'one construct that reaches the destination on every execution of its code'. Under that construct-level reading the tier is 21 constructs, with mifos at 15.

A : B`). title: The tier-reading gate checks only that keys exist
evidence: The census builds the set app:file:line from rows with verdict 'must' and checks only that each must site is listed. The `targets` field of each reading is never compared with the edges' destinations. Stale rows never fail, and two constructs on one line share a key (pushEdge distinguishes by column). The current targets do match: a recomputation from the six DBs finds no mismatch.
consequence: A must construct that is later resolved to a different destination still passes the gate described in ch5:1086-1087 ('the census refuses to report a must construct that file does not list').
fix: Compare each listed site's targets with the set of must destinations its edges reach, and fail on unused rows.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding's description of the code is correct. In graph-census.mjs:103-104, `reading` is a Set of `${app}:${site}` built from rows whose verdict is 'must'. Line 120 computes `unread` from mustSiteKeys (lines 88-91, keyed `${file}:${loc.line}` with no column), and line 121 throws only when a must site is missing from that set. `targets` is never read: grep finds no use of it in any harness script, and graph-census.mjs is the only consumer of tier-reading.json. The check runs one way only, so a row no must site uses never fails. The key ignores the column, while extract.ts:298-299 treats two constructs on one line as distinct (it compares line and col). So a second must construct on a line already listed, possibly with a different destination, would pass. A must construct re-resolved to a different target would also pass, as long as file:line stay the same.

Nothing is wrong in the current results. I recomputed against the six corpus DBs. tier-reading.json has 25 rows, all with verdict 'must' and no duplicate keys. Every must site is listed. Every row's `targets` equals the set of must destinations its witnesses reach. No row is unused. No must site has two different columns on one line.

The thesis also does not overclaim. ch5-results.tex:1098-1099 says only that "the census refuses to report a must construct that file does not list", and that is exactly what the code enforces. The tier-reading.json note says the same.

So the gate is weaker than the readings it guards: it proves a row exists, not that the recorded reading (target, guards) still matches the graph. That is a robustness gap for future re-measurements, not a defect in any reported number or sentence. Hence minor.

title: The REMOVE_GUARD check ignores which guard was removed, and the evidence it relies on is truncated
evidence: `named` is computed from the removed list but used only for the exclusion. check() passes if any edge loses any guard text. delta.guardChanged is stored truncated to 4 entries (line 409), so a DETECTED verdict that depends on a later entry cannot be audited from the result file. All 11 current DETECTED mutants were checked by hand and each loses a guard from the removed list (requireAuth, fn#ddb96242, ViewProfileRuleGuard, PluginEnabledGuard, ExtensionsDataLoaderGuard, deepLinkGuard()/authGuard, organizationPermissionsGuard(), organizationIsUnmanaged), so there is no current misfire.
consequence: The detection rule is looser than the 1.6.0 and 1.7.0 header claims ('loses a guard it carried'). Because guard factories print without arguments, it cannot tell the removed organizationPermissionsGuard() from its two namesakes.
fix: When named is non-empty, require the lost text to be in named. Store the full guardChanged list.

verdict.reasoning:
The facts in the finding about the code are correct. The check at mutate.mjs:297-302 never reads `named`. It passes when any edge's count of any non-null guard text drops, so it does not test that the lost guard is the removed one. That contradicts the operator's own prediction at mutate.mjs:282 ("an edge that carried the guard loses it"), which names the removed guard. delta.guardChanged is cut to 4 entries at mutate.mjs:409, and the console prints detail only for verdicts other than DETECTED. A DETECTED verdict that rested on a 5th or later entry could therefore not be audited from the result JSON.

Parts of the finding are overstated:
(1) "Looser than the header claims" is wrong as written. The 1.6.0 header (mutate.mjs:16-17) and the thesis (ch4-evaluation.tex:487, ch5-results.tex:739) both say "some edge loses a guard it carried", and the check does exactly that. The real gap is with the predict string and with the conclusion in ch5 that "every guard it could observe behaved as the model requires".
(2) The suggested fix only partly works. The `named` regex accepts only bare identifiers or `x()`, so a factory written with arguments never gets into `named`. Bitwarden's `organizationPermissionsGuard(canAccessSettingsTab)` gives `named=[]`. For payment-details, `named` is only `["organizationIsUnmanaged"]`. Requiring the lost text to be in `named` would not tighten the settings mutant at all.
(3) The namesake ambiguity comes from the extractor printing a factory without its arguments. No filter on `named` can resolve it, and ch4:489-492 already states it.

No reported figure changes. All 11 attributed DETECTED REMOVE_GUARD mutants, and the 9 non-attributed ones, can be audited from the first stored entry, and in each the edge loses the guard that was removed. A case where removing guard A makes an edge lose an unrelated guard B under the extractor's router-semantics gating is not shown by any evidence (ASSUMPTION). So this is a real but latent looseness in the harness: severity minor, with no effect on the 11/11 figure.

title: The call-graph prose says factory providers 'contribute no edge', but candidates() resolves such tokens by declared type and counts them
evidence: candidates(t) falls back to 'direct' for any non-abstract app class and to 'subclass' for an abstract one, whether or not the token is provided via useFactory. In bitwarden, core.module.ts:260-261 provides the abstract AutomationCapability (libs/automation-driver/src/automation-capability.ts:15) by useFactory -> new ProcessReloadCapability, a subclass. core.module.ts:304-305 provides WindowStorageService by useFactory. Calls on fields of these types are resolved and counted in \CGDirect or \CGSubclass.
consequence: ch6 tells the reader such calls add no edge and fall back to the injector join. In fact they add edges, possibly to implementations other than the one the factory builds, and they are counted as resolved.
fix: Correct the prose, or treat a token bound only by useFactory or useValue as unresolved and count it in \CGUnresolved.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds, though one of its examples is wrong and the damage is limited. The ch6 prose (ch6-discussion.tex:580-582) says a useFactory/useValue provider "bind[s] nothing the pass can follow, so a call through such a token contributes no edge" and the member "falls back to the join over every component that injects its class". The code does something else. The bindings loop (callgraph.ts:60-68) only reads useClass/useExisting, so a factory-bound token gets no binding. But candidates() (callgraph.ts:78-88) then falls back to the token's declared class: 'direct' if the class is concrete, 'subclass' if it is abstract. The call is counted (callgraph.ts:141) and adds call edges (142-146). The prose only holds for non-class InjectionToken constants: those return null and are not even counted as unresolved. For a class token the prose contradicts the code, and those calls go into \CGDirect/\CGSubclass, which ch6 reports as resolutions.

Corrections to the finding:
(1) The AutomationCapability example does not go through a field of that type. AutomationDriverService has a constructor parameter `capabilities` (@Inject(AutomationCapability), not a parameter property) and a Map field of the same name. fieldTypes (callgraph.ts:108-112) keys both by name, so `this.capabilities.get/set/has/keys` (Map calls) are resolved to AutomationCapability subclasses. get/set happen to match subclass members and produce spurious edges. This is a separate name-collision defect.
(2) The finding says calls may resolve to "implementations other than the one the factory builds". No corpus instance does this. The genuine factory-bound class tokens are WindowStorageService (factory builds WindowStorageService itself), MessageListener (builds MessageListener itself) and ManagedSettingsService (abstract; the subclass set includes DefaultManagedSettingsService, which the factory builds). Each resolves to a superset that contains the factory's product.

Effect on the claims: the join only adds screens, so an extra edge can only widen a member scope. Claim 3.1 and the must tier are untouched. What is wrong is the description of the approximation, plus a few tens of the 7186 counted 'direct' resolutions. So: real, minor, a prose and counting-interpretation error. The fix: qualify the prose ("a class token bound only by a factory is still resolved by its declared type") or count such tokens as unresolved.

title: The sweep figures come from a hand-written JSON that remeasure.sh never re-runs; the gate only matches strings
evidence: covered() checks only that afterAddedTests or result starts with 'killed'. First-pass rows record a test count ('Tests 4 failed') but no test names. remeasure.sh regenerates generated-sweep.tex without re-running any mutant, and the output carries no extractorStamp. In a scratch clone the 9 named killers and 16 first-pass router-semantics mutants (35, 37, 41, 42, 46-48, 50-54, 60, 61, 63, 64) all fail on-topic assertions, so the file is accurate today, but nothing would detect drift if extract.ts changed after a8c7480.
consequence: \SweepCommit and \SweepMutants are regenerated on every remeasure, so they look freshly measured although nothing is re-run. The kill status of first-pass mutants cannot be audited from the record.
fix: Script the sweep: apply each 'what', run vitest with --reporter=json, store the failing test names and a sha of extract.ts, and have sweep-to-latex refuse if that sha differs from HEAD's.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds only as a latent provenance gap. Its line numbers are wrong, its main consequence is refuted, and nothing has drifted yet.

What holds up:
- The gate only matches strings. `sweep-to-latex.mjs:8` reads `covered = (m) => !m.survived || /^killed/.test(m.afterAddedTests ?? '')`, and line 9 applies the same regex to `extra[].result`. The finding cites lines 15-17 and 18-23, but the file has 18 lines.
- `remeasure.sh:61` (not :71; the file has 62 lines) only regenerates `generated-sweep.tex` from the stored JSON and never re-runs a mutant.
- First-pass rows record only a count, for example id 1: "Tests  4 failed | 341 passed (345)", with no test names.
- The other generated files carry a header "% Extractor 0027017, packages/ clean, harness clean when generated." `generated-sweep.tex` has no such header and no check that HEAD's extractor still matches the swept commit.

What does not hold:
1. "Look freshly measured" is refuted. `\SweepCommit` prints a8c7480, not the measurement commit 0027017. `ch5-results.tex:1129-1132` says the mutants deleted rules "from a copy of the extractor at \texttt{\SweepCommit}" and that the survivors "are killed by tests added after the sweep". A reader is told the sweep is a one-off run at an older commit. The title-page line in `thesis.tex:69-70` ("Every figure is re-measured on the commit named in the generated tables") is also met: the named commit is a8c7480, where it was measured. The word "re-measured" sits a little loosely with a figure that `remeasure.sh` does not re-run.
2. Drift is hypothetical. `git diff --stat a8c7480 HEAD -- packages` shows only `packages/adapter-angular/src/panel3.test.ts` (+67 lines). The extractor source is byte-identical between the swept commit and the measured one (0027017/HEAD). The tests were only added to, so a first-pass kill cannot have become a survivor. The present-tense claim that each rule is covered by a test that fails when the rule is deleted therefore holds at HEAD.
3. "Cannot be audited" is overstated. Each row records the exact `what` replacement and the commit, so it can be reproduced and checked. It just cannot be checked by reading test names.

Net effect: no current figure or claim is wrong. The weakness is that the sweep falls outside the "Extractor X, packages/ clean" stamp the other generators carry, so a future change to the extractor would leave stale sweep macros with no warning. That is a process-hardening point, minor at most, and does not affect Claim 3.1 as it stands.
